cases.title: Radial maze errors before and after a hippocampal lesion
cases.context: Researchers interested in spatial memory did a study to evaluate the effect of a hippocampal lesion (surgical damage to the hippocampus, a brain structure used for remembering places) on performance in an eight-arm radial maze. Each rat was evaluated in a test session before the lesion (measurement 1) and again in a test session two weeks after the lesion (measurement 2). The number of working memory errors (entries into an arm that was already visited in that session) was recorded.
tasks: Based on the recorded data, is there evidence that the number of working memory errors is different in these two states? Assume that any quantities of interest are Normally distributed. DO NOT use R.

Provide your result in a single complete sentence that would convey your conclusion in a way that could be understood by a non-expert in statistics or medicine (e.g., a typical reader of a local newspaper).

hypotheses.nullWords: The hippocampal lesion produces no change in the mean number of working memory errors (the true mean after-minus-before difference is zero).
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The hippocampal lesion changes the mean number of working memory errors (the true mean after-minus-before difference is not zero).

cases.symbols: \(d_i\) (difference in subject \(i\)), \(\bar d\) (mean difference), \(s_d\) (SD of the differences), \(s_{\bar d}\) (standard error of the mean difference), \(\delta\) (true mean difference), \(n\) (number of subjects), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom).

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
steps.words: Each rat is measured under both conditions, so the procedure is the paired t test on the within-rat differences. The hippocampal lesion produces no change in the mean number of working memory errors (the true mean after-minus-before difference is zero). The hippocampal lesion changes the mean number of working memory errors (the true mean after-minus-before difference is not zero).

steps.title: Form one difference per rat
steps.words: Subtract in the same direction for every rat (after minus before). Rat 6 has a difference of the opposite sign and it keeps its minus sign. The analysis now uses only these 10 numbers.

steps.title: Calculate the mean difference
steps.words: The mean difference estimates the true mean change \(\delta\) in errors.

steps.title: Calculate the SD of the differences
steps.words: Square each deviation of a difference from the mean difference, add them, divide by \(n-1\), and take the root.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the mean difference
steps.words: The standard error describes how much the mean difference varies from sample to sample.

steps.title: Calculate the t statistic
general: t=\frac{\bar d-\delta}{s_{\bar d}}=\frac{\bar d}{s_{\bar d}}\quad(\delta=0\text{ under }H_0)
steps.words: Under the null hypothesis the true mean difference is zero, so the numerator is the mean difference itself.

steps.title: Find the degrees of freedom and the critical value
steps.words: Start with \(\alpha=0.05\). Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1. Use row 9 and the two-tailed 0.05 column. The printed cutoff is 2.262.

steps.title: Make the decision and bracket P
steps.words: The statistic exceeds the 0.05 cutoff, so reject the null hypothesis. In row 9 it also passes the 0.001 column (4.781), which is the last printed column, so P < 0.001.

cases.conclusion: The mean after-minus-before difference is 3.5 errors, t = 5.09325 with 9 degrees of freedom, beyond the cutoff 2.262. Reject the null hypothesis. There is a difference in the number of working memory errors between the two states (P < 0.001). In plain words, the rats made about three and a half more maze errors per session after the lesion than before it, and this change is larger than chance alone would explain.

cases.title: Speech-in-noise scores with and without a hearing aid, treated as two groups
cases.context: In a study looking at speech understanding in background noise, ten listeners with mild hearing loss repeated lists of 50 words that were played in cafeteria noise. Each listener was tested once without a hearing aid and once with a hearing aid, and the number of words repeated correctly was recorded. An analyst overlooked that the same ten listeners were measured in both conditions and treated the two sets of measurements as two independent groups of ten different people. The table gives the sample size, mean and standard deviation (SD) of each set of measurements.
tasks: Treat the two sets of measurements as independent groups. Based on these summary data, is there evidence that the mean speech-in-noise score is different with and without a hearing aid? Assume that any quantities of interest are Normally distributed. DO NOT use R.
A paired analysis of the same ten listeners gives t = 5.33854 with 9 degrees of freedom. Please state why the two analyses reach different conclusions and which one fits this design.

hypotheses.nullWords: Mean speech-in-noise score is the same with and without a hearing aid.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: Mean speech-in-noise score differs with and without a hearing aid.

cases.symbols: \(\bar x_i\) (group sample mean), \(s_i\) (group sample SD), \(n_i\) (group size), \(s^2\) (pooled variance), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom).

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
steps.words: The unpaired t test compares two group means as if every number came from a different listener. The null hypothesis states that mean speech-in-noise score is the same with and without a hearing aid.

steps.title: Calculate the group means and SDs
steps.words: These are the values in the table. The SDs are large because the listeners differ a lot from one another in speech-in-noise score.

steps.title: Pool the variances
steps.words: Each group variance is weighted by its own degrees of freedom.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error and t
steps.words: The numerator is the same 3.8 words as in a paired analysis, but the denominator now carries the spread between listeners.

steps.title: Find the degrees of freedom and the critical value
steps.words: Start with \(\alpha=0.05\). Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1. Use row 18 and the two-tailed 0.05 column. The printed cutoff is 2.101.

steps.title: Make the decision
steps.words: The unpaired test does not reject the null hypothesis (P > 0.05). The paired test on the same numbers gives t = 5.33854 with 9 degrees of freedom and rejects it (P < 0.001). Pairing removes the large differences between listeners and leaves only the change within each listener, so its standard error is 0.711805 instead of 2.40046.

cases.conclusion: Analyzed as two independent groups, t = 1.58303 with 18 degrees of freedom is below 2.101, so the unpaired test finds no evidence of a difference in speech-in-noise score (P > 0.05). The paired test on the same data finds that there is a difference (P < 0.001). Ignoring the pairing hides the difference because the spread between listeners enters the standard error.

cases.title: Pigeon key pecking under three reinforcement schedules

tasks: Is there a difference in Stroop interference over time? Use a significance level of \(\alpha = 0.05\) for your inference. (Note: If a difference exists, do not identify which groups are different.)
Assume that any quantities of interest are Normally distributed. DO NOT use R.

hypotheses.alternative: H_A:\text{at least one treatment mean differs}
hypotheses.nullWords: Mean Stroop interference is the same at all three times awake.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: At least one time awake has a different mean Stroop interference.

cases.symbols: \(x_{ts}\) (response to treatment \(t\) in subject \(s\)), \(\bar S_s\) (subject mean), \(\bar T_t\) (treatment mean), \(\bar X\) (grand mean), \(m\) (number of treatments), \(n\) (number of subjects), \(SS\) (sum of squares), \(MS\) (mean square), \(F\) (F statistic).

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
general: H_A:\text{not all treatment means are equal}
steps.words: Every subject receives every treatment, so the procedure is repeated measures ANOVA. The null hypothesis is that mean Stroop interference is the same at all three times awake. The alternative is that at least one time awake has a different mean.

steps.title: Calculate the subject means
steps.words: Average across the 3 treatments within each subject.

steps.title: Calculate the treatment means and the grand mean
steps.words: Average down each treatment column across the 4 subjects, then average all 12 observations.

steps.title: Calculate the sum of squares within subjects
steps.words: The spread of each subject around its own mean is added up. Differences between subjects (SS between subjects = 1597.67) are set aside.

steps.title: Calculate the treatment sum of squares
steps.words: The factor n appears because each treatment mean is based on n subjects.

steps.title: Calculate the residual sum of squares
steps.words: What remains of the within-subject variation after the treatment effect is removed is the residual.

steps.title: Calculate the mean squares and F
steps.words: A large F means the treatment means differ more than the leftover within-subject noise would explain.

steps.title: Find the critical F
steps.words: Open F_table.pdf, PDF page 1. Use numerator column \(\nu_n=2\) and denominator row \(\nu_d=6\). The lightface (P < .05) value is 5.14. The boldface (P < .01) value is 10.92.

steps.title: Make the decision and bracket P
steps.words: F exceeds the lightface 0.05 value, so reject the null hypothesis. It does not reach the boldface 0.01 value, so P < 0.05 but not P < 0.01. The result is close to the cutoff.

cases.conclusion: F = 5.44096 with 2 and 6 degrees of freedom exceeds 5.14 but not the boldface 10.92. Reject the null hypothesis. There is a difference in mean Stroop interference among the three times awake (P < 0.05).

questions.stem: For the radial maze errors of ten rats before and after a hippocampal lesion, what is the SD of the after-minus-before differences \(s_d\)?
questions.why: The squared deviations sum to 42.5. Dividing by n − 1 = 9 gives 4.72222 and its root is 2.17307. Dividing by n, skipping the root, or dividing again by the root of n gives the other values.

questions.stem: For the mood ratings of eleven subjects before and after two weeks of bright light therapy, what is the paired t statistic?
questions.why: t is the mean difference 5.54545 divided by its standard error 1.28179. The value 1.84308 is what an unpaired test gives on the same columns, and 1.30444 forgets to divide the SD by the root of n.

questions.stem: For the left ear and right ear tone detection thresholds of ten subjects, the paired statistic is \(t=1.16775\). Which printed critical value is it compared with at \(\alpha=0.05\), and what is the decision?
options: \(t_{0.05}(18)=2.101\), do not reject the null hypothesis
\(t_{0.05}(9)=2.262\), do not reject the null hypothesis
questions.why: There are ten differences, so ν = n − 1 = 9 and the printed cutoff is 2.262. The statistic 1.16775 is below it, so the null hypothesis is not rejected.

questions.stem: For the syllable counts of eleven zebra finches before and after deafening, what is the mean after-minus-before difference \(\bar d\)?
questions.why: The eleven differences sum to -33 and dividing by n = 11 gives -3. The two positive differences keep their signs in the sum, and the divisor is n, not n − 1.

questions.stem: For the speech-in-noise scores treated as two independent groups of ten listeners (with hearing aid mean 30.3, SD 5.12185, without hearing aid mean 26.5, SD 5.60258), what is the unpaired t statistic?
questions.why: The pooled variance is 28.8111, the standard error is 2.40046 and t = 3.8/2.40046 = 1.58303. The value 5.33854 is the paired t on the same data, and the other values leave one or both sample sizes out of the standard error.

questions.stem: For the key pecking rates of five pigeons under three reinforcement schedules, \(SS_{wit\,subjs}=1272.67\) and \(SS_{treat}=1140.4\). What is F?
questions.why: The residual is 1272.67 − 1140.4 = 132.267 with (5 − 1)(3 − 1) = 8 degrees of freedom, so F = 570.2/16.5333 = 34.4879. The wrong values use the within-subjects sum of squares as the denominator, skip the degrees of freedom, or use the wrong residual degrees of freedom.

questions.stem: Twelve listeners each have a speech reception threshold (the quietest level at which half of the sentences are understood) measured with noise coming from the front and again with noise coming from the side. Which analysis fits this design?
options: An unpaired t test on the two columns, with 22 degrees of freedom
A one-way ANOVA with two groups of twelve different people
A z test for two proportions
A paired t test on the twelve within-listener differences, with 11 degrees of freedom
questions.why: The same listeners give both measurements, so the two columns are not independent. The paired t test works on one difference per listener and has n − 1 = 11 degrees of freedom.

questions.stem: Rats differ a lot from one another in baseline lever pressing rate, but each rat changes by a similar small amount after reward devaluation. Why can an unpaired t test on the before and after columns fail to find the change?
options: Its standard error includes the large spread between rats, so the same mean change is divided by a larger number
It uses fewer degrees of freedom than the paired test, so its cutoff is much larger
It compares medians instead of means
It changes the mean difference between the two columns
questions.why: Both tests have the same numerator, the difference between the two column means. The unpaired denominator is built from the spread between animals, while the paired denominator uses only the spread of the within-animal changes.

questions.stem: R prints the line "t = 4.3412, df = 9, p-value = 0.001874" for t.test(after, before, paired = TRUE) on the positive affect scores of ten subjects. Which hand calculation does the t in this line correspond to?
questions.why: R's t is the mean difference divided by its standard error, 3.5/0.806226 = 4.34122. R does not print the SD of the differences or the standard error, and the last option is the confidence interval line.

questions.stem: Six speakers each produce the same words at a slow, a normal and a fast speaking rate, and voice onset time is measured each time. For the repeated measures ANOVA, which degrees of freedom are used to find the critical F?
questions.why: The numerator has m − 1 = 2 degrees of freedom and the residual has (n − 1)(m − 1) = 5 × 2 = 10. The value 15 would be right only if the eighteen measurements came from eighteen different people.

notes: All data are invented for practice. Printed critical values were read from sources/tables/t_table.pdf page 1 (rows 9, 10, 18, 20) and sources/tables/F_table.pdf page 1 (columns 2, rows 6, 8, 10). No df row had to be bracketed.

Outcomes. Reject: maze lesion (P < 0.001), light therapy (P < 0.002), birdsong (P < 0.05, close to the 0.05 cutoff), exercise mood in R, pigeon schedules (P < 0.01), Stroop sleep loss (F just above the 0.05 value, not above the 0.01 value). Do not reject: ear tone threshold (paired), voice onset time (repeated measures), and both unpaired analyses by design.
Every paired table has at least one difference of the opposite sign.

The two s20unpaired cases keep the ref layout (summary table of the two columns). Three keys were added to their values beyond the ref key set so the check script can recompute from raw scores and the paired comparison can be shown. raw1 and raw2 are the raw scores of group 1 and group 2 in subject order, and pairedT is the paired t (group 1 minus group 2) quoted in the second task.
The s20pairedR output in values.rOutput was produced by running Rscript (R 4.6.1) on the case data. The solution words describe the output in sentences because colons are not allowed in words.

Colons and semicolons are avoided in words and conclusion, and the t table step adds Start with alpha = 0.05. After the style review the tag about not identifying groups is written in his exact form with its Note label, and the R task uses his wording, so the check script allows colons and semicolons in context and tasks only.
values.exactP is stored as in the ref cases but exact P values are not quoted in the solutions, except the R p-value in the s20pairedR case.
